questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Visiting Australia was always something that excited me, so I chose the country and then the university after.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
My exchange was amazing! I met so many amazing people, made a ton of friends, had exciting courses and got to travel around the coutry.
My only regret is that I could only go for one semester and that I had to leave all my friends behind.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
It was quite a challenge.
Because Australia is so far away there was significant time delays every time I contacted the university.
Also, the way ANU does things are totally different from KU so there was a lot of adjustment.
Australia is also quite hard to get into, so having all papers, vaccines etc. prepared was a massive task that took hugh amounts of my time.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
The university hosted a series of information and social events.
The friends I made at the student hall were also helpful.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer:
Going on exchange is a MASSIVE undertaking!
Do not underestimate the amount of time you will spend preparing.
Sometimes it seems like it won't be worth it, but it definetly will!

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
I lived in a student hall.
ANU has accommodation guarantee, but you cannot pick which student hall to go to.
Some student halls can cost more than 500AUD a week(!). I lived in the cheapest which cost only 250AUD a week.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer:
The is a shared kitchen in the main block, where all 500 students from the student hall cook at the same time.
The kitchen is quite old and worn and there is not a lot of storage space assigned to each student.
However, it is a great opportunity to meet new friends.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
Do it!
It's a great way to meet people and the vibe on campus is amazing (like a small city).
It's also great for getting to class easily.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I lived in Burton and Garran Hall, which is the cheapest and oldest student hall.
The facilities are definitely worn, but the social aspects more than compencate for this!
I met my best friends in the kitchen, coached badminton, participated in social activities and had so many good memories.
There were always something going on from parties, open mics, karaoke, sport events etc.
Honestly, even though it might be cheaper finding off-campus housing I highly recommend spending the extra to give yourself the student hall experience in Australia - it is totally different from in DK!
To be honest, student halls work much better in Australia.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
It was too technical with not enough support.
I spent ages going over what felt like a billion websites and pdf documents to figure out what I was doing.
ANU also cancelled all my courses two weeks before I left for Australia...

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
I cannot remember everything anymore, but there was a lot of deadlines and things to fill out before.
Also, ANU uses many different websites which makes it all very confusing. 
The time difference also meant that I had to get up in the middle of the night sometimes to do odd jobs.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: ANU has a support mail, but it was very slow and the time difference did not help.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
I was succesful, only problem was they cancelled all my courses. 
It is also a very slow process, and ANU can be a bit hard to convince that you fulfill the pre-requisites.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Take it slow!
Start early!
And write down everything! Make "to-do lists", write notes contact ANU do everything to make it as easy as possible for yourself and make sureyou don't forget something or have to go through hundreds of documents again to find what you are looking for.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
The lecturers were excellent and the courses super interesting.
There were very few scheduled classes and lectures, which meant you had to study alone a lot more and because ANU has such a large population from Asia (where they don't make study groups) it can be hard to find someone to study with.
Also, tutorials were only 1 hour, so you never finished all the assigned questions, which meant you felt a bit underprepared for the exam.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The level was very fitting (maybe a bit easy sometimes compared to KU).
However, ANU does very poorely in describing the course-content. 
I signed up for what I though was introduction to Game Theory but turned out to be introduction to Advance Game Theory, because ANU does a lot of Game Theory during their micro courses. Also, the lecturer was a math graduate from MIT, so the course was extremely math-heavy, went fast and had lots of assumed knowledge.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Less scheduled classes and lectures (i.e. you have to study more at home).
People don't show up for the lectures, so be prepared for the lecturers to directly ask those who show up. Once you've gotten used to this though it is nice since they learn your name and take a direct interest in your learning.
Also the tutorials are just going through the answers to questions, so you have to prepare everything beforehand.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- The World Economy since 1800
- Development, Poverty and Famine
- Behavioural Economics
- Game Theory

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Behavioural Economics was super interesting and professor Simon Grant was really engaging (many found him a bit heavy on notation though).
Also, Development Economics is super relevant and professor Martine Mariotti did super well in relating course material to the real world and assign interesting articles for the course.
I would highly recommend these two courses!

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
There were many events and social activities that cost money - though I highly recommend going.
Also, you want to experience Australia and everyone flies everywhere, but with rising petrol costs it is VERY expensive. 
Most national parks also cost money to go to.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Food is more expensive in Australia.
Mobile phones are really expensive as well.
I spent less on transport than expected, but probably because I lived in Canberra and bought a bike early on.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
So many clubs and societies on campus!
Also, the student hall arranges tons of activities.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Every kind of sport, board game societies, cultural societies, academic clubs - they had everything.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Board game nights were really fun and a great way to meet people.
Also sign up for some student hall sporting events or become a coach (I coached badminton), since you will also meet a lot of people this way.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Go to Tasmania! So beautiful!
Tidbinbilla nature park is nice, War Memorial in Canberra is interesting and the parliament building is very impressive.
I also recommend getting a bike and exploring Canberra and especially biking around lake burley griffin.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It took a while to make friends, but Australians are very friendly and outgoing, so it wasn't a big problem.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Join a student hall and just talk to people.
Also participate in many O-week events, even if it seems scary.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
Australians go out clubbing a lot, which I don't really like.
But I found friends who didn't go out too often, so that suited me very well.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
The people and the rich history of the indigenous people.
I highly recommend attending a "welcome-to-country"-ceremony

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
- Be open to everything.
- Join a student hall.
- Prepare yourself to cry when you leave and have to say goodbye to your friends.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Engage with your lecturers. They really appriciate someone talking to them about things other than marks or extensions for assignments and they give back what you give them.
Also say yes to everything in the beginning. It can be exhausting but you will make a lot of friends and the you can relax a bit later on in the semester.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The friends I made.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Saying goodbye to my friends and Australia - it is such an amazing country.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer:
Go on exhange!
But know that it is a LOT of work.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
